reverse_outline.summary: Chapter promise: learn seven questions that distinguish methods from cards and write a per-family rule for acting after success
Key points: one API unifies start and status but not meaning; success promises differ per method; the two providers name the same reversal differently
The three failure patterns addressed: card logic misapplied, debit counted as paid too early, returned debit nobody can classify
Opening case: a direct-debit membership shown as paid bounces five days later, with no warning in the stored status
Thesis: an API can unify starting and status reporting but not what success means, because schemes fix that, so a rule per method family is needed
Treating every method as a card costs money in access, payouts and reporting
Places the chapter in the running example: it covers the method choice before the card journey and asks how other methods would have changed it
Roadmap of the chapter's sections in order

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: Paid Until It Was Not ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Femke finds nearly half of Larkfield's volume is non-card, yet one card-style rule governs what 'paid' permits for every method

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: Paid Until It Was Not ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: That rule caused three direct-debit symptoms: access granted then withdrawn, money leaving balances after payout, and returns miscounted as disputes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: Paid Until It Was Not ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The real question is what may be done after 'paid' for each kind of method, not which methods to offer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Seven Questions That Separate a Method From a Card ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Defines payment method and scheme, and argues that the provider-defined family, not the brand, is the unit to design for

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Seven Questions That Separate a Method From a Card ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Families differ on seven properties whose answers decide what is allowed after success; a table contrasts the card answers with other families

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Seven Questions That Separate a Method From a Card ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Push versus pull is the root distinction, since pulls stay revocable and pushes mostly do not / defines account-to-account payment and finality as terms that follow from it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Seven Questions That Separate a Method From a Card ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: A pull rests on a mandate that must be recorded and producible, and its cancellation may only be learned through a failed payment
'Succeeded' describes the method's process, not the money's safety, so the promise must be read family by family (with the order of reading announced)
Bank redirects such as iDEAL and Bancontact are pushes with an immediate answer, no hold and no bank dispute, as both providers document
For SEPA direct debit the law gives the payer two distinct rights: an eight-week no-reason refund and a thirteen-month unauthorized claim
Providers confirm those rights and add that the direct-debit outcome arrives days later and returns cannot be contested
Other direct-debit schemes work the same way with different numbers, and for ACH the providers' figures conflict and could not be verified against the scheme rules
A wallet is not a family for these purposes: some are cards underneath and keep card rules, others are schemes of their own, so the scheme rather than the button decides
'Real-time' means speed between banks and implies neither finality nor availability of funds to the merchant, shown by EU instant transfers, FedNow and Pix
Wero illustrates the same gap: a bank's guarantee comes first and the funds in a later step that can fail, and the scheme is still changing
Vouchers sit at the slow extreme: the API response is only an instruction to pay, and the outcome may come days later or never
Outside cards a refund is a separate payment in reverse with its own window, delay and failure mode

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How One API Presents Them: A Stored Instrument or a Parameter ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Providers can unify the start request, the next-action instruction and the status channel; what remains is how the method itself is represented

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How One API Presents Them: A Stored Instrument or a Parameter ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe represents the method as a stored instrument object, uniform at the top but method-specific beneath, even in whether it can be reused

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How One API Presents Them: A Stored Instrument or a Parameter ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe by default also chooses which methods are offered, so an integration can start accepting a method its code never named

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How One API Presents Them: A Stored Instrument or a Parameter ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen names the method as a request parameter / which methods are available is a matter of account configuration the merchant requests

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How One API Presents Them: A Stored Instrument or a Parameter ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Both providers document per method whether there is a hold to capture, and their answers for the same method can differ

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How One API Presents Them: A Stored Instrument or a Parameter ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Both abstractions leak in the same four places (capture, refund, reversal naming, timing of success), each one of the seven questions showing through

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How One API Presents Them: A Stored Instrument or a Parameter ¶7
reverse_outline.summary: How providers actually reach each method is largely undisclosed, with only traces of third parties, so the chapter describes the documented contract only

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Handle the Differences in Your Own Code ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Three ways to handle method differences in code: act on status alone, branch on method name, or keep a policy table per method family

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Handle the Differences in Your Own Code ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces the comparison table: the three designs trade first-day effort against resilience to methods being added, renamed or migrated

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Handle the Differences in Your Own Code ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Whether to offer a revocable method is a pricing decision: direct debit is about half the cost but returnable, so use it for recurring payments to known customers

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces a table gathering the documented Stripe/Adyen differences and what each demands of the integrator's code

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Provider-specific advice: on Stripe guard against methods the code has never seen; on Adyen classify chargeback events by reason code; on both answer the seven questions per method page

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: A Rule per Method Family ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield now stores the method family with each payment and uses one table to decide paid, access and reversal horizon / justifies the 'open-ended' Bacs entry from the scheme guarantee and Stripe's page

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: A Rule per Method Family ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Worked example: one SEPA debit traced through pending, confirmation and its two reversal deadlines, which Larkfield stores and weighs against the studio's balance

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: A Rule per Method Family ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Because providers label the same return differently, Larkfield classifies reversals under four own terms, so the dispute report counts only genuine disputes
Failure one: a redirect payment succeeds but the customer never returns, so fulfilment must rely on the webhook and a sweep of pending payments
Failure two: a debit reported collected fails later and the provider deducts it at once, so the merchant must monitor money still in its reversal window and re-collect
Failure three: a merchant refund plus a bank claim credits the customer twice, preventable only by telling the customer the refund is coming
Failure four: a scheme migration (iDEAL to Wero) hits a whole method by deadline, so migrations should be scheduled and the seven questions re-answered
Established takeaways: method properties come from schemes and law, 'succeeded' describes the flow only, and real-time is speed not finality
Context-dependent takeaways: when to offer direct debit, when to let the provider choose methods, and when to grant access before confirmation
Author's recommendations: store family and reversal horizon and let a table decide next steps, and keep your own reversal vocabulary
Checklist of eight questions to ask about each method and provider
Methods vary in whether the customer must act and when the outcome arrives, which one status word cannot express; hands off to the state-machine chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 46 aligned units' outline summaries match the controlling ideas of p01 to p46 in spec order; the three introduction callouts match no spec paragraph.

Three units were marked two_ideas (p11, p26, p35). p11: the terms account-to-account and finality are consequences of push or pull, as the spec declares. p26: one topic sentence covers Adyen's parameter and configured list as one design set against Stripe's. p35: the Bacs sourcing is support for a cell of the table the paragraph presents. None holds two controlling ideas.

Every body unit ties to a supporting claim S1 to S5 as its section declares; p04, p05 and p46 are orienting or transitional units. p32 (whether to offer direct debit) ties to S5 only loosely; its placement is ruled on under flow_is_followable.

Each table is introduced or followed by a sentence saying what it sets out, the three figures carry captions stating what they show, and quotations are framed by a sentence of interpretation (for example 'A canceled permission is learned from a failure', 'Both say that the confirming message is the webhook').

All declared transitions are expressed at their boundaries (for example 'Her question needs a vocabulary', 'Adyen, by contrast', 'So both abstractions leak', 'The leaks land in your code', 'Even with the rule in place'). The one-api opening states only the new half of its contrast, but both flow readers placed the section without difficulty.

The introduction opens on a concrete puzzling case, states a disputable thesis and gives a roadmap; none of the weak patterns applies.
The conclusion sorts its points by how settled they are, restates no new evidence beyond recap, and ends on a hand-off the spec declares; no weak pattern applies.

The author's synthesis states the verb/promise observation ('The provider owns the verb (start, report) and the scheme owns what was promised, so a status alone is half of the payment') and the stakes: who carries the returns, and a fraud report written by the providers' words.
The membership paid on the 1st and returned on the 6th comes back: `paid` was never the right word on day one and the return is named a failed collection.

The cold reader predicted all eight sections in the roadmap's order, the Larkfield case, scheme and law facts, the provider comparison and a plain practical tone; the only gap is that cited sources were not foreseen.

The answer lists outcome timing and confirmation by webhook, no hold to capture, how a refund travels and whether it fails, and whether the payer can take the money back and until when, plus the customer's action and order expiry: more than four of the expected questions, with nothing contradicting.

The answer says the two words name the same scheme event, that an unpaid debit is a failed collection and not a dispute, that the sum overstates disputes, and that the integration needs its own terms separating failed collection, payer refund claim and unauthorized-debit claim.
